st.headline: Why parents need to be involved in the money conversation with their children
st.teaser: A $5 experiment and a playground trip taught me that good money habits require time and effort.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Shopping with real money helps children become more financially savvy.
This thought crossed my mind while volunteering on a shopping trip with UOB Heartbeat volunteers on July 22.
I was paired with UOB’s Ho Ying Ying and Najwa Chua, 12, who has participated in these outings since she was eight.
We began by reviewing the shopping list that Najwa had put together with her parents, before taking a short walk to FairPrice at Rivervale Plaza.
Najwa went about getting the items on her list: bananas, grapes, 30 eggs, chicken and bread.
Since the chicken was on sale, she picked up two packets. After all, her family loves curry chicken.
However, she had to forgo her favourite Lay’s sour cream potato chips because they did not fit her budget. Instead, she opted for two packets of FairPrice house-brand chips, which were on sale.
Najwa tried to keep a running tab in her head, but got overwhelmed as her shopping basket filled up, and she asked to borrow Ho’s phone to check the final sum.
Her careful budgeting left her enough to buy a bottle of Thai sweet chilli sauce that her parents love. Her final bill came to $49.98, within the $50 she was allocated.
It was clear that Najwa actively looked out for deals and knew which brands offered more bang for her buck.
She shared that she had picked up budgeting skills and practical tips from the volunteers during previous shopping stints.

A spokesperson from Children’s Wishing Well, the charity leading this financial literacy initiative, said that these hands-on experiences and interactions with the volunteers have helped Najwa become more confident in making spending decisions.
Today, she knows how to manage her money and adapt her choices to stay within her budget – and not just on these organised shopping runs.
Her mother has even entrusted her with the family’s weekly provisions, allowing her to head to the supermarket after school to buy the items on her own.
Hearing how much Najwa has grown, I thought: “Why not try this out on my daughter?”
She is in Primary 2 and will turn eight later in 2026.
I started by increasing her daily allowance for school meals to $5, which she can use for both her morning snack and lunch.
The experiment is still a work in progress.
While her school has taught her about needs and wants, she still tries to justify her wants as a need.
Once, she spent $2.50 at the bookshop on a mechanical pencil and pencil leads.
When I asked why she bought them when she had normal pencils, she replied, “I need the mechanical pencil to write.”
My daughter chose to spend on her perceived “need”. With only $2.50 left for the day, she spent $1.80 on two cheese sticks for her morning snack and decided to skip lunch – which to me is a “need”.
Hoping to drive home the “needs versus wants” lesson through play, my husband and I decided to take our daughter to explore Curiosity Cove.

During our visit, my husband observed that the financial literacy elements at Curiosity Cove are more of a sideline, and the educational concepts are relegated to “secondary amusement” for the children after they finish playing.
Venturing outside Curiosity Cove, we spotted some activity stations around the Mandai area.
One station focusing on needs and wants required children to build a virtual buggy. To do so, they had to decide which car parts they needed to buy and which parts they could skip.
Another station touched on savings and interest. By shifting a marker on a slider board, children can see how interest grows as their savings increase – so the more they save, the more they earn.

However, these displays would not automatically spur any meaningful discussion or learning unless parents step in to talk about the concepts, using the posters to convey the financial lessons to their children.
Banks are offering digital tools to keep that dialogue going.
Nelson Neo, DBS’ head of retail banking and head of POSB, noted that the Smart Buddy app enables parents to keep tabs on their children’s spending.

cna.headline: Probation for motorcyclist, 21, who performed dangerous 'Superman' stunt while riding along ECP
cna.teaser: GoPro footage found by police on the motorcyclist's own camera showed him lying prone on the bike with his feet off the rear controls for at least 16 seconds.
fullText: SINGAPORE: A 21-year-old man who performed a motorcycle stunt along the East Coast Parkway (ECP) was sentenced to 15 months' probation on Wednesday (Oct 7).

Mohamed Asfa Mohamed Azli, a Singaporean, had stretched out his body and lay flat in a prone position on the bike, in what court documents called a "Superman stunt" that was dangerous to other road users.
His actions came to light when a traffic police officer found footage of the stunt which Asfa had recorded on his GoPro camera.
Asfa had pleaded guilty on Apr 17 to one charge of reckless driving. Another charge for not wearing a helmet while riding a motorcycle was taken into consideration.

As part of his probation terms, he has to remain indoors from 10pm until 6am, and will have to perform 40 hours of community service. He is also barred from obtaining any driving licence or driving any vehicle during his probation period.
His parents have also been required to put up a S$5,000 (US$3,909) bond to ensure Asfa's good behaviour during his probation term.
According to court documents, Asfa was riding his motorcycle with several friends from Seah Im car park in the Keppel area to a car park at East Coast Park on Aug 31, 2025 at around midnight.
He had fixed a GoPro 360 camera on the handlebar of his motorcycle, and began recording while on the ECP.

On the ECP, he performed the "Superman" stunt twice by lying prone on the seat with his body and legs straightened, parallel to the road. The video showed he had ridden in this position for at least 16 seconds and overtaken two vehicles while performing the stunt.

Court documents stated that while Asfa was performing the stunt, he could not have engaged the rear brake or engine brake of the motorcycle as his feet were not on the rear brake pedal or gear shifter.
In doing so, he had also raised the centre of gravity of himself and the motorcycle, making it more likely he would lose his balance, the prosecution added.
While at the East Coast Park car park, several traffic police arrived as part of their patrol routine. In a panic, Asfa fled the scene, leaving his camera on the motorcycle.
His actions came to light when a traffic police officer reviewed the footage from the unattended camera as part of investigations into the gathering.
After Asfa's guilty plea, the court called for a report to see if Asfa was suited for probation.
While the initial report found him unsuitable for probation due to several factors like his unwillingness to change, later reports found that he has exhibited positive changes in his behaviour.
A reformative training suitability report had found that Asfa's family provided a supportive environment for him, and that he had ceased contact with the peers associated with his offence.
Reformative training is a harsher type of penalty involving a regimented rehabilitation programme for youth offenders.

Given his improved behaviour, Deputy Public Prosecutor Johan Tay sought 15 months' supervised probation for Asfa, as well as a prohibition on him driving during the probation period, and a requirement for him to serve 40 hours of community service.
Mr Tay also asked for Asfa's parents to put up a good behaviour bond.
For reckless or dangerous driving, Asfa could have been jailed for up to a year, fined up to S$5,000 or both.
